opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think for me the value of a physical theory is not so much that it's "true" in some absolute sense, but that it compresses a huge amount of phenomena into a small number of ideas you can actually reason with. A good theory tells you what matters and, just as importantly, what doesn't matter. In statistical physics that's really the heart of it: you have systems with an astronomical number of degrees of freedom, and yet their large-scale behavior is controlled by a handful of quantities, symmetries, dimensionality, conservation laws. The notion of universality, that very different microscopic systems end up behaving the same way, is to me one of the deepest lessons physics has to offer.

So when I think about a theory as a tool, I ask a few things. Does it make predictions that are quantitative and can fail? Does it identify the right variables, the right scaling, so that you can collapse messy data onto simple curves? And does it give you intuition you can carry to new situations, rather than just fitting what you already saw? A theory that explains everything after the fact but predicts nothing isn't very useful.

That's also why I find it natural to bring this way of thinking to machine learning. Deep networks are, in a sense, complex systems with many interacting parts, trained on data with rich structure. The empirical side moves incredibly fast, but we still lack a clear understanding of why these methods work, why they beat the curse of dimensionality on real data, for instance. The physicist's approach is to build simplified models of data, models that are tractable but retain the essential structure, like hierarchy or locality, and then see whether they reproduce the scaling laws we observe in practice. If they do, you've learned something about which properties of the data are responsible for learnability. If they don't, that's informative too.

So in the end, I'd say physical theories are valuable because they are a disciplined way of simplifying. Not simplifying arbitrarily, but finding the simplification that survives contact with experiment.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a very good question, because I come from physics, and in physics we have a certain culture about what a theory is supposed to do. And I would say the value of a theory is not really that it predicts everything. It's that it tells you what matters and what does not matter.

If you think about something like the theory of phase transitions, or more generally statistical physics, you have systems with an enormous number of degrees of freedom, maybe ten to the twenty-three particles, and you cannot follow all of them. And yet you can say very precise things, because it turns out that most of the microscopic details are irrelevant. There are a few quantities that control the behavior, and once you have identified them, the picture becomes simple. So a good theory is a compression. It tells you which variables to look at, and it gives you a language to ask the right questions.

I think this is exactly the situation we are in with machine learning. You have these neural networks with billions of parameters, and people train them, and they work, and nobody really understands why. And there is a temptation to say, okay, it's an engineering object, it's too complicated, let's just do experiments. But that was also the situation with many physical systems before we had the right concepts. For me the goal is not to write down an equation that reproduces GPT. The goal is to find the few quantities that control, for example, how the test error decreases with the number of data, or why the network learns some features before others, or what kind of structure in the data makes learning possible at all. If you can identify that, you have understood something, even if you cannot compute everything from first principles.

And I would add one more thing, which is that a theory is also valuable because it can be wrong. If I have a scaling argument that says the error should go like the number of samples to some power, with an exponent that depends on some property of the data, I can go and measure it, and if it does not work, I have learned something. That is what makes it a tool and not just a story. In machine learning we have a lot of stories, intuitions about why things work, and I think the physicist's contribution is to try to turn those into statements that can be tested quantitatively, sometimes on very simplified models that we can actually solve, and then see what survives when you go to the real thing.

astra-6.text:
I think the value of a physical theory is that it allows you to understand something complicated in terms of a small number of principles. You have to simplify, of course. The world has an enormous number of details, and if you try to include all of them, you may reproduce what you observe without really understanding why it happens.

So the question is: which details matter for the phenomenon you want to explain? A good theory makes that distinction. It might be inaccurate in some respects, but still capture a mechanism that gives you predictions you can test. And ideally, it explains why systems that look quite different behave in similar ways.

For me, that is the power of physics. You construct a simplified description, work out its consequences, and confront them with observations. When it fails, you have an opportunity to learn which assumption was wrong, or which ingredient you were missing. So a theory is useful both for what it explains and for making precise what we do not yet understand.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the value of a physical theory is that it allows you to understand which details matter and which details you can forget. The world is very complicated, and if you try to describe everything at once, you may not understand very much. So you construct a simplified model, and you ask whether it captures the phenomenon you want to explain.

What is remarkable is that sometimes a very simple description works for many systems that look quite different microscopically. Then you have learned something: the behavior does not depend on all those microscopic details. It depends on a few properties that these systems share.

Of course, the simplification has to be tested. You want predictions, ideally predictions you did not put into the model at the beginning. And when the theory fails, that is useful too, because it tells you that something you neglected is actually important. So I see a theory as a way to organize our understanding and make it precise enough that we can discover where it is wrong.
